text: CSV is flat — one customer's three orders mean that customer's name gets repeated three times. JSON can nest, and this lesson shows you how to move between the two, plus a quirk that catches almost everyone: the numbers that started in your CSV are still strings once they land in JSON.

orders is the exact same list of twenty dictionaries DictReader gave you last lesson. json.dump writes that list straight to a file as JSON, and indent equals two just makes the output readable instead of one unbroken line. But look closely at quantity and unit_price in the result — they're still quoted, still strings, because DictReader never converted them and json.dump had no numbers to write.

json.load is the mirror of json.dump — it parses a file's JSON text back into Python lists and dicts. If you only have a JSON string already sitting in memory, say from an API response body, you'd reach for json.loads instead, the string version.

A flat CSV can't express one customer, many orders without repeating that customer's name on every single row, which is exactly what orders.csv does. defaultdict of list collects every order under its customer_id without you having to check whether the key exists first, and json.dumps here is just pretty-printing the result to the terminal.

Four names, and the pattern that keeps them straight. The file versions, dump and load, read and write an open file object. The string versions, dumps and loads — the s stands for string — read and write a string you already have in memory. Get that distinction and you'll never confuse them again.

Real data isn't always clean, though. Next lesson is exception handling — try, except, and raise — using the exact bad rows this chapter keeps finding, a missing customer name and a negative quantity, to build a pipeline that survives bad data instead of crashing on it.
